approach:
Two stages, deliberately split at the line where the data stops being trustworthy.

STAGE 1 - MECHANICAL, runs on what we have. Build a monthly cross-section over NSE EQ-series names that have a balance sheet. Apply hard filters (survival, solvency, real profit, tradeability), then rank the survivors on a NEGLECT score that has been residualised against size, plus sector-appropriate cheapness and a capital-return quality measure. Output ~25-30 names.

The residualisation is the whole trick and it is not decoration. I measured it: log turnover correlates 0.91 with log market cap, average ticket size 0.86, filing count 0.59. A naive "low attention" screen is a market-cap screen wearing a costume, and he already owns the small-cap factor by construction. So attention is measured as the RESIDUAL from a regression of log(daily trade count) and log(12m filing count) on log(market cap): how quiet is this company relative to what a company of its size normally gets. Residual-vs-size correlation is 0.000 by construction, residual standard deviation 0.77 (trades) and 0.37 (filings), so there is real spread left after size is removed. I dropped the turnover residual: it correlates 0.92 with the trades residual and adds nothing. Two inputs, not three.

I sanity-checked the score by looking at its wrong end. The most-attended names by this measure came back as ANGELONE, OLAELEC, CAMS, IXIGO, ZAGGLE - exactly the loud, heavily-covered names. The construct separates crowded from quiet within a size bucket, which is what it claims to do.

STAGE 2 - MANUAL, roughly 15 names, one evening each. Because three things the strategy depends on cannot be automated from this data and pretending otherwise is how the last backtest lied: the sector label (missing for 59% of symbols, and for 132 of the 203 screen survivors), the promoter pledge level (we have an event feed, not a percentage), and the share count (derived, and wrong by >25% for 13.5% of names, concentrated in exactly the low-EPS small caps being targeted). At 25-30 names, hand-checking is cheap. At 500 it would be impossible - which is another way of saying the screen's job is to get the list small enough to do properly.

ON THE GRID SEARCH: he asked for a limited one, and there is a hard constraint he should hear plainly. There is nothing to optimise against. No historical fundamental panel exists, so no configuration can be scored on return. What a grid CAN do here is test membership stability. Vary three parameters (market-cap band, neglect cut, anti-rally lookback) across three levels each = 27 configurations, and keep only names appearing in two-thirds or more of them. A name that qualifies under one setting and vanishes under the next is a parameter artifact, not an idea. Log all 27 to state/trials.jsonl via zen/validation/trials.py so the trial count stays honest for anything measured later.
thesis: Neglect is the one inefficiency a Rs 5 lakh account can actually harvest, because it is the only one where his constraint is the source of the edge rather than a tax on it. A fund running Rs 500 crore cannot take a meaningful position in a Rs 600 crore company without moving it and cannot justify an analyst's salary against a position that size, so those companies go unpriced by anyone who does serious work. Rs 50,000 is invisible in a name doing Rs 20 lakh a day. The premium being claimed is a payment for doing research nobody else is paid to do, and for accepting illiquidity he does not actually suffer from. That is a structural gap rather than a statistical pattern, which matters because statistical patterns in this dataset have already failed once - the volume anomaly measured worse than random. But the honest form of the claim is narrow: neglect is a NECESSARY condition for mispricing, not a sufficient one. Most quiet companies are quiet because they are bad, and the base rate is unforgiving - only 42.6% of liquid names beat the Nifty 500 over twelve months and the median lags it. So the neglect score does no work on its own; it defines a pond where the odds of a mispricing being left alone are better than average, and the quality and valuation filters do the actual separating. The design earns its keep only if those filters are strict enough to reject most of the pond.
hard_filters: SURVIVAL: NSE series EQ only, excluding BE (the surveillance/trade-for-trade bucket - 18,031 recent rows). Traded on at least 150 of the last 250 sessions, with zero-volume days permitted (I checked: no name in the recent EQ universe has a zero-volume session, so this is a guard, not an active filter).

TRADEABILITY: median daily turnover at least Rs 15 lakh, i.e. 30x a Rs 50,000 position. This corrects a premise worth stating - impact cost is NOT automatically negligible at his size. The 10th percentile of median daily turnover is Rs 2.78 lakh, where Rs 50,000 is 18% of a day's trade. The claim holds comfortably above roughly Rs 10-15 lakh a day and not below it. 1,637 of 1,957 names clear this.

SIZE: market cap between Rs 300 crore and Rs 5,000 crore. Below Rs 300 crore the reported numbers stop being reliable enough to filter on and the share-count error explodes; above Rs 5,000 crore the neglect premise is gone. Cuts 1,637 to 807.

LEVERAGE: debt_to_equity at or below 1.5 on the most recent half-yearly balance sheet, no exceptions, no averaging. His hard limit. 3,342 of 3,489 names with a computable ratio already pass, so this is a tail-cutter rather than a real screen - but it is the tail that kills portfolios. Cuts 807 to 734.

REAL PROFIT: profit_normalised > 0 AND ebitda > 0 on the latest period. profit_normalised strips exceptional items, which is the right base - a neglected small cap booking a land sale into net profit is the single most common way this screen would get fooled. Cuts 734 to 607.

SOLVENCY: current_assets / current_liabilities >= 1.0. Available on the half-yearly balance sheet (45.4% fill, which is the balance-sheet subset). A neglected company that cannot fund its own working capital is not neglected, it is dying quietly.

EXCLUDE BANKS AND NBFCs ENTIRELY. This is a real exclusion, not a technicality - Finance is the third-largest industry by symbol count in the announcements feed. The XBRL tag set we parse is manufacturing/services-shaped (RevenueFromOperations, CostOfMaterialsConsumed, EmployeeBenefitExpense); it does not capture net interest income, provisions, gross NPA or capital adequacy. We cannot compute P/Adjusted-BV, so any bank valuation from this data would be fabricated. Better to own no banks than to own one on a made-up number.

NOT ALREADY DISCOVERED: no exchange volume/price clarification query (announcements category='volume_query') in the last 12 months. 580 symbols tripped one in the past year; if the exchange has noticed the price action, so has everyone else.
ranking_factors: NEGLECT (size-residualised), weight 40%. Mean of two percentile ranks: the residual of log(median daily trade count) and the residual of log(12-month filing count), each regressed on log(market cap). Lower is more neglected. These two residuals correlate only 0.34, so they carry genuinely different information - trade count is how many people are participating, filing count is how much the company itself is saying. The turnover residual is deliberately excluded as redundant (0.92 correlation with the trades residual).

CHEAPNESS versus sector peers, weight 30%. Percentile rank of the sector-appropriate multiple WITHIN the industry peer group, never across the whole market. Asset-light and stable businesses: P/E on annualised profit_normalised. Capital-intensive: EV/EBITDA. Ranking within-sector rather than across it removes most of the need for a sector-neutral construction elsewhere.

CAPITAL RETURN, weight 20%. EBITDA divided by (equity + debt_total), annualised, as a ROCE proxy - every input exists on the half-yearly balance sheet. Judged against a 10-12% Indian WACC; below 12% scores zero rather than scoring low, because a neglected company earning under its cost of capital is not a bargain at any price.

BALANCE-SHEET DIRECTION, weight 10%. Change in debt_to_equity from the March filing to the September filing. Falling leverage scores well. This is the weakest factor in the set and it is weak for a stated reason: two observations is not a trend, it is a line segment. It breaks ties and nothing more.

EARNINGS QUALITY, as a veto rather than a weight. exceptional_items divided by pbt over the available quarters. If the gap between profit_reported and profit_normalised is large or erratic, the company is dropped from the ranking rather than penalised in it. Also drop any name where the latest filing has audited = false and the two prior quarters disagree materially with it.
entry_rule:
He wants to be early, not late, and he explicitly does not want momentum. The gate is therefore relative and carries no free threshold: the name's 6-month return must be BELOW THE MEDIAN of the screened universe over the same window. Stated as a percentile rather than a fixed percentage, this costs zero tunable numbers and stays valid in any tape - in a bull market "below median" is still a positive number, which is correct, since demanding an absolute decline would only buy in crashes. On the prototype this cut 413 names to 203, so roughly half the neglected-and-solvent set is already moving and gets excluded.

That gate alone builds a falling-knife portfolio, so it is paired with a staged entry that also fixes the impatience problem:

TRANCHE 1 - half the position (Rs 25,000) on qualification. He buys while it is quiet and unloved, which is the entire point.

TRANCHE 2 - the other half only after the next results filing lands (detectable in the announcements feed, category='results', on trade_date), and only if revenue and profit_normalised have not deteriorated versus the filing he bought on. If they have, the position stays at half size permanently and the exit rules run against the half.

The second tranche is timed by the reporting calendar rather than by price, which keeps it from becoming a momentum rule through the back door. It also does real behavioural work: it gives him something structured to do in the waiting period, which is when his stated failure mode - impatience - actually operates. He is not sitting on his hands; he is waiting for a specific, dated, external event.

One hard sequencing constraint: no entry may be made on fundamentals older than two reported quarters. As of today that rule blocks the entire screen, because the freshest data is the September 2025 half-year and it is September 2026. This is not a caveat to note and move past - the screen cannot be run at all until the December 2025, March 2026 and June 2026 filings are backfilled.
exit_rules: WRITTEN AT ENTRY, ON THE TICKET, AS RUPEE PRICES - not as rules to be interpreted later. Every position gets a physical entry card with four numbers filled in before the buy order goes in: stop price, first target, second target, and expiry date. His failure mode is deciding in the moment, so the moment must arrive with the decision already made.

HARD STOP: close 25% below the entry price, executed the next session, no averaging down, no 'let me see one more quarter'. In a 10-position book at Rs 50,000 each, one stopped-out name costs 2.5% of capital. That is survivable arithmetic, which is exactly why the stop must be honoured while it is cheap.

RE-RATING EXIT - the discipline for winners, which is the half he historically got wrong. He bought a discount to sector peers; when the discount closes, the reason to own it is gone regardless of how good the story now sounds. Sell half when the sector-appropriate multiple reaches the peer-group median RECORDED AT ENTRY (a fixed number on the card, not a moving one that can be rationalised upward), and the rest at 1.25x that level. Selling in two pieces is a concession to psychology: full exits feel irreversible and get postponed, half exits get taken.

CROWDING EXIT: the neglect residual moves from the bottom tercile into the top tercile. The premium being harvested was the neglect itself; once the crowd arrives, the position has become a momentum holding he never intended to own. The screen's own entry variable becomes its exit trigger, which is a nice property - it means the thesis and the sell signal are the same measurement.

TIME STOP: 24 months. If the name is still neglected, still cheap, and earnings have not grown, the thesis did not fail loudly - it simply did not happen, which is the outcome that produces years of dead capital. Twenty-four months is long enough that a genuine re-rating has had time and short enough that it does not become a permanent holding by default.

THESIS-BREAK EXIT, immediate and non-negotiable, no tranching: debt_to_equity crosses 1.5 on any half-yearly balance sheet; a filing appears in announcements category='pledge' that management has not explained within 30 days; an auditor qualification; or a promoter sale. These are the four ways a neglected small cap goes to zero, and each is detectable in the announcements feed within a day.

ENFORCEMENT: the exit ledger runs in jobs/daily_brief.py, which already exists, and reports breaches to him as facts rather than as questions. The system must never present an exit as a decision, because presenting it as a decision is what re-opens the door his stated failure mode walks through.
data_we_lack: FUNDAMENTALS ARE STALE. Latest period_end is 2025-09-30 and max broadcast_dt is 2025-12-05, against today's date of 2026-09-08. The screen cannot be run right now on anything current - it needs the Dec-25, Mar-26 and Jun-26 filings first. Buying on a year-old balance sheet in a leveraged small cap means buying blind through exactly the window in which leverage builds.

NO TTM EARNINGS AND NO YEAR-OVER-YEAR ANYTHING. I checked the distribution directly: the maximum number of income-statement quarters for any symbol is 3 (Mar/Jun/Sep 2025); 1,415 symbols have 3, 725 have 2, 55 have 1. Trailing-twelve-month profit cannot be computed for a single company. Neither can any YoY growth rate. Sequential quarter-on-quarter is all that exists, and Indian quarters are seasonal enough that Q/Q comparisons are close to noise. Every P/E in this design is an ANNUALISED quarter, which is a genuinely worse number than a TTM and will misprice any seasonal business.

NO ANALYST COVERAGE DATA. None, in any form. The 'thin coverage' leg of the brief is proxied by trade counts and filing counts, which is a different thing measured badly. If this design has a soft centre, it is here.

NO SHAREHOLDING PATTERN. No promoter percentage, no FII/DII holdings, no free float, no institutional turnover. 'Low institutional turnover' is proxied by average ticket size (turnover divided by trades), and that proxy correlates 0.86 in logs with market cap - meaning it is mostly measuring size, not institutional presence. Residualising helps but does not create information that was never collected.

PROMOTER PLEDGE LEVEL IS NOT AVAILABLE, only pledge EVENTS. announcements category='pledge' has 4,187 filings across 1,542 symbols all-time but only 231 symbols in the last 24 months, and each row is a subject line, not a percentage. His hard limit on pledging therefore CANNOT be enforced mechanically. It must be hand-checked per shortlist name, and that check is not optional.

NO MEDIA PRESENCE DATA AT ALL. The announcements feed is regulatory filings, not press coverage. This leg of the brief is unbuildable from what exists and I am not going to substitute filing counts for it and call it media.

NO INDEX CONSTITUENT LISTS. The indices table holds price series only (18 indices, OHLC, no membership). 'Not in the Nifty 500' - the single cleanest and most defensible definition of institutional neglect - cannot be computed. This is the most valuable missing field in the whole design and it is probably the cheapest to add.

SHARE COUNT IS DERIVED, NOT REPORTED. Market cap comes from close x shares_implied, where shares_implied = profit / EPS. I validated it against BSE market caps via ISIN (n=1,901): median relative error 1.6%, correlation 0.978 in logs - good. But the tail is bad and it is the wrong tail: 13.5% of names are off by more than 25%, 6.7% by more than 50%, and the errors concentrate in low-EPS names (median error 5.8% for |EPS| under 0.5 versus 0.8% above 5). Those low-EPS names ARE the neglected small caps this screen targets. Every market cap and every P/E on the final shortlist must be checked by hand against the BSE file or a filing.

NO SECTOR LABEL FOR MOST OF THE UNIVERSE. announcements.industry is populated for 1,040 of 2,527 symbols (48.3% of rows, 75 distinct values, one of which is '-'). On my prototype funnel it was the single most destructive filter: 203 survivors fell to 71 on the requirement of having any industry label at all. The 3-per-sector cap cannot be automated. It must be assigned by hand on the shortlist.

NO CASH BALANCE TAG. The XBRL set gives assets and current_assets but not cash and equivalents specifically, so enterprise value must use GROSS debt. EV/EBITDA is therefore overstated for cash-rich companies - and net-cash, under-covered small caps are precisely the profile this screen is hunting. The bias runs directly against the strategy's own thesis.

NO BACKTEST IS POSSIBLE. Not hard - impossible. Two comparable balance sheets exist (1,387 symbols have both Mar-25 and Sep-25). Nothing in this design has been measured against returns and nothing can be until several more years of filings accumulate. Every expected-return statement here is a prior. The only quantitative validation available today is the parameter-stability check described in the approach, and that tests robustness of the name list, not profitability.
data_required: financials: period_end, broadcast_dt (point-in-time gate, never period_end), consolidated, audited, revenue, ebitda, profit_normalised, profit_reported, exceptional_items, pbt, eps_basic, shares_implied, equity, debt_total, debt_to_equity, assets, current_assets, current_liabilities, finance_costs, has_balance_sheet
prices: date, symbol, series (EQ vs BE), close, volume, turnover, trades - trades is the load-bearing one for the neglect residual and is 100% populated on recent data
announcements: symbol, trade_date, category (pledge, volume_query, results, governance), industry, subject
universe.json: ISIN_NUMBER and Mktcap, joined to prices.isin_code, as the independent cross-check on derived share counts (hits 2,285 of 2,741 recent EQ ISINs)
indices: Nifty Smallcap 100 and Nifty 500 closes, for relative-return measurement and the anti-rally percentile gate
corpactions: split and bonus adjustment factors, so the 6-month return gate is not fooled by an unadjusted split
NOT AVAILABLE, must be sourced or hand-collected: index membership lists, shareholding patterns, promoter pledge percentages, analyst coverage counts, a sector map, and cash balances
sector_handling:
Sector does three separate jobs here and the data supports exactly one of them.

WHICH MULTIPLE TO USE - works, given a sector label. P/E on annualised profit_normalised for asset-light and stable businesses (IT services, mature consumer). EV/EBITDA for capital-intensive names (telecom, infra, steel, cement, airlines, hotels, hospitals) where depreciation policy distorts earnings - and every input exists: ebitda is populated 96.4%, debt_total on the balance-sheet subset. P/B and P/Adjusted-BV for banks and NBFCs is NOT supported, because the tag set has no interest income, no provisions, no gross NPA and no capital adequacy. Hence the recommendation to exclude financials outright rather than value them on invented inputs.

PEER-RELATIVE RANKING - works, and is where sector earns most of its keep. Cheapness is ranked within the industry group rather than across the market, so a screen does not simply fill up with whichever sector is currently out of favour.

THE 3-PER-SECTOR CAP - does NOT work automatically, and this is the sharpest gap in the design. announcements.industry covers 1,040 of 2,527 symbols, and on the prototype funnel it cut 203 survivors to 71. Automating the cap on that field would silently discard two-thirds of the qualifying universe for the sole reason that nobody tagged them, which has nothing to do with their merit.

The fix is to stop trying. Run the screen WITHOUT any sector requirement, produce 25-30 ranked names, then assign sector by hand - using the NSE industry label where it exists as a first pass and the company's own description otherwise. Twenty-five lookups is an hour of work, once a month. Apply the 3-per-sector cap at that point, on the ranked list, taking the highest-ranked names in each sector.

Two things worth flagging on the cap itself. First, the NSE labels are too granular for the purpose - 'Textiles - Cotton', 'Textiles - Synthetic' and 'Textile Products' are three separate labels and, for concentration-risk purposes, one sector. They need collapsing into roughly 12 economic groups by hand before the cap means anything. Second, and more important: the cap controls sector risk but not the risk that actually dominates this book. Ten neglected Indian small caps across ten different sectors still share one enormous common factor, which is the small-cap tape itself. When it turns, they correlate regardless of sector. The 3-per-sector rule is worth keeping and should not be mistaken for diversification.
how_it_could_fail:
The most likely failure is the dullest one: neglect is usually deserved, and the quality filters are not strong enough to tell the difference. The base rate is already known to be hostile - 42.6% of liquid names beat the Nifty 500 over 12 months and the median lags it - and the neglected small-cap pool is a worse-than-average draw on governance, not a better one. Every quality filter here leans on numbers the promoter reported about himself, unaudited in three quarters of four. The screen's entire defence against a fabricated set of accounts is that exceptional items look tidy, and that is not much of a defence.

Second: the neglect residual may be measuring liquidity provision rather than attention. A stock with few trades might have no market maker and a wide spread, in which case the 'premium' is a bid-ask cost being collected on the way in and paid again on the way out - a transaction tax mistaken for alpha. Nothing in the data distinguishes these, because there are no intraday quotes.

Third: the anti-rally gate manufactures value traps by design. Selecting names in the bottom half of 6-month returns, that are cheap, and that nobody is trading, is a precise recipe for catching falling knives. The staged entry blunts this and does not remove it. Expect a meaningful fraction of positions to stop out at -25%, and expect them to do so in clusters.

Fourth - the correlation problem. Ten positions at Rs 50,000 makes a single -60% name cost 6% of capital, which is fine. But three small caps in a bad small-cap tape can cost 25%, and the sector cap does not control for the factor that actually drives that. He should size his expectation of drawdown off the small-cap index, not off ten independent bets.

Fifth, and most concrete right now: the fundamentals are nine months stale. Screening on September-2025 balance sheets in September 2026 means every leverage and solvency filter is answering last year's question. For a leveraged small cap, that is precisely the interval in which a thesis quietly breaks.

Sixth, the parameter-stability check can only ever confirm that a name is robust to my arbitrary choices. It cannot confirm the name is good. Robust and wrong is entirely available, and if the 27-configuration grid is ever described as validation, this design has started lying the same way the 30% CAGR backtest did.

But the single point of failure is behavioural, not statistical. Every edge claimed here is conditional on the exits being executed mechanically. If he overrides the -25% stop once - and the moment it happens will feel like the one obviously justified exception - the design reverts to the exact pattern he described: holding losers because selling crystallises the mistake, selling winners early because gains feel fragile. No amount of screen quality survives that. The screen is the easy part; the entry card with four numbers already written on it is the part that actually has to work.
